blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en:
Cooperative 3D tracking must integrate complementary observations
across agents and time while maintaining consistent identities.
When evidence integration and identity inheritance share
a matching decision, errors arising from cross-view appearance
differences and spatial misalignment can compromise both
feature fusion and track continuity.
We propose FFBL-Coop, a fuse first, bind later framework
that separates instance admission from identity management.
Confidence-ranked Slot Admission (CSA) allocates cooperative queries
to available ego slots using confidence and spatial proximity.
Unified Representation Aggregation (URA) uses cooperative
semantic features and aligned anchors to guide ego-feature
retrieval, refining the augmented query bank within a shared
transformer decoder.
After refinement, Cooperative-Priority Identity Anchoring
(CPIA) combines learned association with persistent mappings
to establish accepted identity assignments across frames.
A shared codebook reduces transmitted payload while retaining
AP and AMOTA close to the uncompressed variant.
FFBL-Coop achieves AMOTA/AP of 0.611 / 0.548 0.611/0.548 on V2X-Seq
and 0.688 / 0.653 0.688/0.653 on Griffin-25M.
Code will be released.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en: Cooperative 3D tracking extends ego perception through observations from nearby vehicles, roadside infrastructure, or aerial platforms. These complementary views reveal objects obscured or outside the ego field of view. Exploiting this coverage over time requires integrating incoming evidence while preserving identities across changes in viewpoint and visibility.
blocks.zh: 合作3D跟踪通过附近车辆、路边基础设施或航空平台的观测,扩展自我感知。 这些互补的观点揭示了那些被遮蔽或超出自我视野的物体. 随着时间的推移,利用这种覆盖面需要综合收到的证据,同时在观点和可见度的变化中保留身份。

blocks.en: Intermediate fusion supports evidence integration by exchanging learned representations, such as bird’s-eye-view (BEV) features ( Xu et al., 2022 ; Xu et al., 2023 ) . To reduce communication cost, recent systems exchange sparse object queries and combine cross-agent association with feature aggregation ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Zhong et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) . Within this sparse formulation, SparseCoop and Long-SCOPE accommodate unmatched queries, and SparseCoop further refines representations using ego image features ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026c ) . Incorporating these representations into a recurrent tracker also requires deciding which trajectories the updated hypotheses continue.

blocks.en:
Cooperative integration and temporal tracking impose different
requirements on association.
Specifically, integration must admit useful cooperative evidence
despite cross-view appearance differences and alignment errors,
whereas tracking must preserve identity across frames.
Yet when one cross-agent match controls both query placement
and identity inheritance, a correspondence error can compromise
both representation updates and trajectory continuity
(Figure 1 (a)).
Crucially, uncertainty about which existing track an observation
corresponds to does not necessarily eliminate its value
for detection.
This distinction motivates our principle: integrate and refine cooperative evidence first,
then bind the resulting hypotheses to persistent trajectories .

Following this principle, FFBL-Coop separates evidence admission
from ego-track identity assignment through a fuse first, bind later pipeline.
CSA selects cooperative queries by confidence and spatial proximity
and places them in available ego slots without assigning ego IDs.
URA then uses their semantic features and aligned anchors
to guide ego-feature retrieval and refine the augmented bank.
Only after final decoding does CPIA resolve identities
using refined ego states and persistent cross-agent mappings,
independently of admission weights.
Learned association links queries to existing tracks,
accepted assignments and new-track identities are recorded
in persistent ID mappings.

This separates the decision to integrate an observation

and CPIA combines association with persistent mappings
to maintain identities across slot changes. • Experiments on V2X-Seq and Griffin-25M demonstrate the effectiveness of FFBL-Coop for cooperative 3D detection and tracking.

AP and AMOTA close to uncompressed transmission.

blocks.en: 2.1 3D Multi-Object Tracking
blocks.zh: 2.1 三维多物体跟踪

blocks.en:
Tracking-by-detection methods maintain trajectories by
associating per-frame detections using geometric and motion
cues ( Weng et al., 2020 ; Yin et al., 2021 ) .
A complementary line of work learns object representations
through queries.
Specifically, query-based 3D detectors such as
DETR3D ( Wang et al., 2022 ) and PETR ( Liu et al., 2022 ) aggregate multi-view image features into sparse object queries.
Extending this representation across time,
StreamPETR ( Wang et al., 2023 ) and
Sparse4D ( Lin et al., 2023 ) incorporate historical
information into object-centric representations,
providing a foundation for recurrent updates.

Beyond temporal feature aggregation,
query propagation also supports identity maintenance.

and association within decoder layers.
In a cooperative setting, recurrent updates additionally
incorporate queries maintained by another agent.

identity inheritance using persistent cross-agent ID mappings
to support continuity across slot changes.

blocks.en: 2.2 Cooperative Perception
blocks.zh: 2.2 合作观点

blocks.en:
Cooperative perception extends an agent’s coverage by
incorporating observations from other viewpoints.
Within this paradigm, intermediate fusion exchanges learned
features to integrate complementary evidence.
F-Cooper ( Chen et al., 2019 ) studies feature-level fusion,
while V2X-ViT ( Xu et al., 2022 ) and
CoBEVT ( Xu et al., 2023 ) use attention to aggregate
multi-agent representations.
To make communication more selective,
When2com ( Liu et al., 2020 ) and Where2comm ( Hu et al., 2022 ) use learned communication decisions and spatial confidence
maps, respectively.
Complementing these efficiency-oriented designs,
CoAlign ( Lu et al., 2023 ) addresses pose uncertainty
through agent and object alignment.
At the object level, UniV2X ( Yu et al., 2025 ) exchanges
sparse queries for cooperative perception and planning.

blocks.en:
Building on sparse representations, several methods combine
cross-agent association, ture refinement, and temporal
propagation ( Zhong et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026c ) .
CoopTrack uses graph-based affinities and Hungarian matching
to aggregate paired queries.
SparseCoop combines geometric and appearance cues,
refining queries with ego-image context.
Long-SCOPE uses contextual descriptors and optimal-transport
matching for long-range association.
Despite advances in matching and refinement, coupling identity
inheritance to query allocation can let matching errors affect
both evidence integration and track continuity.
FFBL-Coop addresses this coupling through a fuse first, bind later pipeline that separates feature admission from identity inheritance and records accepted assignments as persistent cross-agent ID mappings.

blocks.en: The perception frontends use specific spatial representations and expose the same query interface ( f , a , s , id ) (f,a,s,\mathrm{id}) for cooperation. Roadside units construct BEV features, while ego vehicles and aerial agents sample image features through projected 3D anchors. Coordinate alignment and feature adaptation are applied before cross-agent integration.

blocks.en: Each agent processes its images with a backbone and feature pyramid network (FPN), producing multi-scale features F t I F_{t}^{I} . blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
In this work, we present FFBL-Coop, a fuse first, bind later framework that separates cooperative evidence admission
from identity inheritance.
CSA allocates cooperative evidence, URA guides ego-feature retrieval
with cooperative semantics, and CPIA combines learned association
with persistent ID mappings to bind identities after refinement.
Together, these stages integrate complementary observations
while supporting tracking continuity across changes in
query placement.
On V2X-Seq and Griffin-25M, FFBL-Coop improves detection
and tracking with compact feature transmission.
Ablations support decoupled identity management,
while perturbation studies show comparatively stable
tracking despite reduced detection accuracy.
Future work will explore uncertainty-aware association
and identity coordination across multiple agents under
changing visibility and connectivity.

depend on the surrounding allocation and identity configuration.

blocks.en:
CoopTrack ( Zhong et al., 2025 ) ,
SparseCoop ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , and
Long-SCOPE ( Wang et al., 2026c ) develop cross-agent
association and feature refinement using graph affinities,
geometric and appearance cues, or contextual matching.
FFBL-Coop builds on these mechanisms through fuse first, bind later : CSA allocates remote evidence,
URA refines hypotheses with ego observations, and CPIA
resolves identities using persistent mappings, learned
association, and new-track initialization.
Its distinction lies in separating query placement from
identity inheritance within the recurrent pipeline,
rather than introducing unmatched-query retention
or ego-image refinement as new capabilities.

blocks.en:
Performance depends on cooperative coverage, detection
quality, and calibration.
In-region refinement relies on useful ego observations,
while out-of-region concatenation retains cooperative
localization errors.
Persistent mappings depend on consistent source IDs
and may propagate accepted identity errors.
Evaluation primarily concerns cars, broader category
coverage remains to be validated.

blocks.en:
Calibration and latency remain limitations despite
comparatively stable AMOTA under the tested conditions.
A 1 ∘ 1^{\circ} yaw perturbation reduces V2X-Seq AP/AMOTA
from 54.8 / 61.1 54.8/61.1 to 49.4 / 60.4 49.4/60.4 .
At 200 ​ ms 200\,\mathrm{ms} latency, Griffin-25M AP decreases
from 65.3 65.3 to 59.4 59.4 , while AMOTA changes from 68.8 68.8 to 68.4 68.4 with velocity compensation.
These evaluations assess the complete pipeline and
do not isolate individual robustness mechanisms.
Reported query payload rates exclude packet headers
and codebook synchronization, so deployment traffic
depends additionally on update frequency and protocol overhead.
Less reliable calibration, variable delays, packet loss,
and identity coordination across multiple agents
remain directions for future work.
